Since then, the legislators of numerous planning grants, referred to earlier, have continued to recognize the economic interdependency of cities and peripheral areas, as evidenced by the requirement that coordinated, comprehensive planning be performed as a qualification to recognize the amount of coordination that is required may be sensed from the fact that there are more than 20,000 units of local government in the SMSA's. 20/
A look at the highway systems in metropolitan areas and associated developments exposes the interfaces between cities and outlying territories. Metropolitan dispersal takes several forms. Most evident is the widening sprawl of suburbs outwards along improved highways and new expressways. Less obvious, but equally important, is the spread of the city's commuting area far beyond these suburbs, so that an increasing proportion of the scattered population is rural non-farm, or involves part-time farmers. The character of previously independent central places is transformed when the market served changes in this way. New outlying shopping plazas are constructed, and business ribbons extend along highways. In short, the areas brought within expanding metropolitan regions are influenced by new locational forces and forms of interdependence, so the classical patterns of the central-place hierarchy break down and are replaced by business patterns characteristically internal to cities. 21/
Urban areas are dynamic, functional systems characterized by complex interrelationships in which the role of transportation is critical. The effect of the automobile on urban structure is not felt only at the urban fringe. In order to speed traffic through the city and into the CBD, most North American cities are criss-crossed with limited access highways and expressways. These make it possible for the suburban dweller to visit the CBD without seeing much of the old central city. Thus the conditions of the central city are hidden behind the concrete canyons of the expressway until dramatic events bring these conditions into the public eye. 22/ The greatest single movement of workers was from one outlying area to another, rather than from the periphery to the core (Vance, 1964, p. 68). 23/
